config.prompt: Two flavours of variation — file each case:

items.label: a smooth range: many genes plus environment
distinct categories set by one or a few genes

config.why: Continuous variation shows a smooth range; discontinuous falls into distinct categories — and only variation written in DNA gives selection anything to filter.

activities.anchor: There is a deeper cut too
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the cut that matters
activities.name: evoInheritCloze

config.text: %%0%% variation is written in DNA and inherited — the only kind selection can act on. %%1%% variation is not: a well-fed child grows taller, but their children inherit %%2%%, not %%3%%.
config.hint: One kind is in the library; the other is in the circumstances.

activities.anchor: the fit can be studied like engineering
activities.caption: pair each example with its adaptation type
activities.name: evoAdaptMatch

config.prompt: Structural, physiological or behavioural — pair each example:

pairs.left: the cactus: spine leaves, a water-storing stem, shallow spreading roots
antifreeze proteins in Arctic fish blood
migration and being active at night in hot climates
the camel's fat hump and heat-tolerant cells
haemoglobin variants keeping oxygen delivery high at 4,000 m

config.why: Body architecture, inner chemistry, actions — three kinds of good fit, all inherited, all filterable.

activities.caption: file the evidence by its line
activities.name: evoEvidenceBuckets

config.prompt: The consensus is built from four converging lines — file each piece:

items.label: Ambulocetus and Rodhocetus — whale ancestors with legs
the pentadactyl pattern in whale flipper, bat wing, human hand
Tiktaalik, found in 2004 in 375-million-year-old Arctic rock
the broken vitamin-C gene (GULO) shared with other primates

config.why: Evolution observed, not inferred — plus inherited furniture from common ancestors and molecular clocks that match the fossil dates independently.

activities.anchor: the way the theory of gravity does
activities.caption: true or false — fitness and theories
activities.name: evoTheoryJudge

statements.s: In this theory, fitness means leaving surviving offspring — nothing stronger or more moral.
statements.why: A slower, weaker variant that raises more young to breeding age is fitter than a magnificent one that does not.

statements.s: 'Survival of the fittest' means the strongest individuals win.
statements.why: Fitness is reproductive success — peacocks' tails, camouflage and antibiotic resistance obey the same arithmetic.

statements.s: In science, a theory is the top of the hierarchy: a framework that explains and predicts across every relevant observation.
statements.why: A hypothesis is the guess; the theory is what the guesses were checked against.

statements.s: Calling evolution 'only a theory' makes it a guess.
statements.why: It is observed in real time, tested against fossils, genomes and biogeography, and has survived 150 years of attempts to break it.

activities.anchor: The worked case is Darwin's finches
activities.caption: rebuild the allopatric fork
activities.name: evoAllopatricOrder

config.prompt: One lineage becomes thirteen — put the allopatric sequence in order:
items: One ancestral finch species reaches the Galápagos islands
The islands differ in seed hardness and rainfall
Isolated beak populations specialise on their island's seeds
Occasional inter-island colonisation hardens the differences
Thirteen species — each a different answer to 'what is a seed here?'
config.why: A barrier cuts gene flow, the halves drift under different selections and luck, and reproductive isolation finishes the fork.

activities.anchor: needed because the peacock's tail is absurd
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the sexual-selection answer
activities.name: evoSexualSpot

config.prompt: This sexual-selection answer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Sexual selection was Darwin's own addition, needed because the peacock's tail is absurd for survival.
Traits that win mates can spread against survival cost when mating success varies more than survival.
The peacock's tail is an honest signal — only a genuinely fit bird can afford the handicap.
Species that form harems show huge male–female differences; pair-bonding species barely differ.
The mechanism runs different steps from natural selection, so its outcomes are unrelated to fitness.
config.correction: It is the SAME four steps with a different filter — mating success IS reproductive success, so its outcomes are fitness by definition.
config.why: Stag antlers (male–male combat) and bird song (female choice) obey the same compounding arithmetic as any other selected trait.

activities.anchor: how fast can populations adapt to climate change?
activities.caption: the sieve's race — run the decision
activities.name: evoClimateBranch

config.root: Selection is a sieve, not a prophecy: whether a population survives rapid change depends on the variation it holds and the time it is given.

start.text: A long-lived tree population faces a warming climate that moves faster than its generations. Which lever is real?

choices.label: Wait for new beneficial mutations
choices.feedback: Mutation is a constant drizzle — a human child carries roughly 60–100 new ones — but slow for one specific beneficial letter.

choices.label: Draw on standing variation and gene flow
choices.feedback: Recombining existing alleles, plus migrants from warmer populations, is the fast route.

choices.label: Assume the sieve guarantees survival
choices.feedback: The four-step mechanism has no foresight — and no guarantee.

wait.text: Drizzle, not a tap — the waiting time for one specific letter can outlast the species.

stand.text: This is how most observed adaptations ran — beak depth shifting in one generation from variation already present.

nope.text: Corals, trees and polar bears are in a race between generation time and environmental change — the sieve may not catch everyone in time.

config.why: Small gene pools make it worse: cheetahs and island species carry little variation, which is precisely what leaves them unable to adapt when disease or climate shifts.
